content: 1. SIMCOR should not be substituted for equivalent doses of immediate-release (crystalline) niacin. When transitioning patients from immediate-release niacin to SIMCOR, therapy should begin at a dose of 500/20 mg and be titrated appropriately to achieve the desired therapeutic response. 2. Patients already taking simvastatin 20-40 mg who require additional lipid management may start SIMCOR at a dose of 500/40 mg once daily at bedtime. Doses of SIMCOR exceeding 2000/40 mg are not recommended. 3. The AIM-HIGH trial, a randomized placebo-controlled study of 3414 patients with stable, previously diagnosed cardiovascular disease, evaluated the effects of niacin extended-release in combination with statin therapy. Baseline lipid levels were LDL-C 74 mg/dL, HDL-C 35 mg/dL, non-HDL-C 111 mg/dL, and median triglycerides 163-177 mg/dL. Ninety-four percent of participants were on background statin therapy prior to the trial. 4. All participants received simvastatin (40-80 mg/day) with or without ezetimibe (10 mg/day) to maintain LDL-C levels between 40-80 mg/dL. They were randomized to receive either niacin extended-release (1500-2000 mg/day) or a matching placebo. The trial was stopped after a mean follow-up of 3 years due to lack of efficacy. 5. Simvastatin can occasionally cause myopathy, characterized by muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness with creatine kinase (CK) levels exceeding 10 times the upper limit of normal (ULN). Myopathy may progress to rhabdomyolysis, with or without acute renal failure secondary to myoglobinuria, and rare fatalities have been reported. 6. Risk factors for myopathy include advanced age (≥65 years), female gender, uncontrolled hypothyroidism, and renal impairment. The risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis is dose-dependent, with higher incidences observed at 80 mg/day compared to lower doses. 7. Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), a rare autoimmune myopathy associated with statin use, has been reported. IMNM is characterized by persistent proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK levels despite statin discontinuation, and improvement with immunosuppressive therapy. 8. Patients starting SIMCOR or increasing their dose should be informed of the risk of myopathy, including rhabdomyolysis, and advised to report any unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, particularly if accompanied by malaise or fever. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if myopathy is diagnosed or suspected. 9. Liver dysfunction, including severe hepatic toxicity and fulminant hepatic necrosis, has been reported in patients substituting sustained-release niacin for immediate-release niacin at equivalent doses. SIMCOR should be used cautiously in patients with a history of liver disease or significant alcohol consumption. 10. Active liver disease or unexplained transaminase elevations are contraindications to SIMCOR use. Liver enzyme tests should be obtained before initiating therapy and repeated as clinically indicated. If serious liver injury occurs, therapy should be promptly discontinued. 11. Niacin therapy can increase fasting blood glucose levels. Diabetic or potentially diabetic patients should be closely monitored during SIMCOR therapy, particularly in the initial months. Adjustments to diet, hypoglycemic therapy, or discontinuation of SIMCOR may be necessary. 12. Niacin can reduce platelet count and cause small increases in prothrombin time (PT). Elevated uric acid levels have also been reported with niacin therapy, and caution is advised in patients predisposed to gout. 13. Small dose-related reductions in phosphorus levels have been observed with niacin in clinical studies, though this effect was not seen in a 24-week simvastatin-controlled study with SIMCOR. 14. Increases in HbA1c and fasting serum glucose levels have been reported with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, including simvastatin.
